Exception Fallacy

While most rules have exceptions, generalisations are formed because a large body of evidence suggests a pattern that is statistically true. The "exception proves the rule" fallacy concludes based on a sample of that group, when the sample is a poor representation of the group.

For example, if you had a cat that liked to swim and you used your swimming cat as the sample to represent all cats, concluding that all cats like to swim. The sample in this case is too small and ends up misrepresenting the group because the swimming cat is the exception, not the rule.

Even if all the premises are true, exception rhetoric ignores important evidence (e.g. one cat out of many and the fact that cats have a reputation for avoiding water). It overlooks the rule and focuses only on the exception.

In either case, the argument is weak because the odds do not support the likelihood of the conclusion being true.
